paragraphs.text: THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

1.	The Applicant, Ms. Thanh Huong Pellegrino-Osei, is a citizen of Vietnam. She applied for a study permit to attend a two-year diploma program in Business Analytics at a designated learning institution in Hamilton, Ontario. On August 11, 2025 a visa officer at the Canadian visa office in Manila refused her application under paragraph 216(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (IRPR) because the officer was not satisfied that she would leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay.

2.	The refusal letter is a template. The only reasons beyond it are in the Global Case Management System (GCMS) notes, which state that “the purpose of the applicant’s visit is not consistent with a reasonable temporary stay given the details provided in the application” and that “the proposed program of study is not reasonable given her career path.”

3.	The Applicant holds a bachelor’s degree in accounting (2021) and has worked as an accounts assistant for four years. She was accepted into the program, paid the first-year tuition deposit and submitted a study plan explaining that analytics skills would let her advance to a senior analyst role at her current employer, who also wrote a letter confirming that her position would be held.

4.	She showed funds of CAD $42,000 in a savings account for more than six months and evidence of family property in Ho Chi Minh City. Her application was supported by letters from her parents and her employer.
5.	(a) Was the officer’s conclusion on the program of study unreasonable? (b) Did the officer’s failure to give adequate reasons breach procedural fairness?

6.	Visa officer decisions are reviewed for reasonableness under Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 10, 23–25. Visa officers are entitled to deference, but their reasons must show a rational chain of analysis (Vavilov at para 102) and must bear “the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility” (Vavilov at para 99).
B. The officer’s conclusion on the study plan was unreasonable

7.	To be granted a study permit, an applicant must show that she is a bona fide student and will leave at the end of the authorized period: section 11(1) and paragraph 20(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA), and paragraph 216(1)(b) of the IRPR. Officers may consider whether a program makes sense in light of the applicant’s background, but they cannot do so on a speculative basis: Solopova v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 690 at paras 10–11.

8.	As described above at para 3, the study plan explained the connection between the program and the Applicant’s employment. The officer’s statement that the program was “not reasonable given her career path” does not engage with this explanation or with the employer’s letter. That is a failure of the sort identified in Vavilov at para 128: the reasons must be responsive to the evidence and submissions.

9.	The officer also did not refer to the Applicant’s funds, which were more than sufficient, or the family ties in Vietnam. Ibid. A decision that ignores central evidence cannot be said to be transparent or intelligible.

10.	Although a visa officer’s duty of fairness is at the low end of the spectrum, the Applicant is entitled to know why her application was refused: Hassani v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1597. The Court has held that the GCMS notes form part of the reasons; here, the notes are barely longer than the template. In Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at para 43, the Supreme Court recognized that written reasons are required in circumstances where the decision has important significance for the individual. A refusal that ends a long-planned education is of such significance.
11.	The Applicant also notes that, under the Vavilov framework, “the reasons must reflect the stakes” (para 133).

12.	The Applicant seeks an order setting aside the refusal dated August 11, 2025 and returning the matter to a different visa officer for redetermination. She also asks for her costs, if special reasons exist under rule 22 of the Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules.
